tools.description:
Run one pixel-art command on a drawing or image you already made. This is
the engine's own command line: it checks work, explains it and improves it.

Commands: check and explain (read-only):
- lint <id> [--rules outline_gap,orphan_pixel,…] — pixel-art defects, each
  naming the node and command that drew them
- inspect <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1 --scale 10 — a zoomed crop with its
  exact colours
- measure <id> --at x,y — what is at a pixel and who drew it
- explain <id> — resolved geometry, per-command footprints, before rendering
- motion / storyboard / silhouette / reveal / clusters / parts <id> — reports
- score <id> — a 0-100 pixel-art discipline score with a breakdown
- compare <id> <id> — two results side by side
Improve (returns a NEW drawing id):
- shade <id> --band 2 --light=-1,-1 — banded shading along a colour ramp
- selout <id> — selective outlining; reoutline / clean-lines / aa / mirror
- cluster <id> --at x,y --action recolor --color <name> — one guarded cluster
- repair <id> — deterministic cleanup of drift, strays, fringe and noise
Sheets and frames (returns a NEW image id):
- split <image> --grid 3x3 — a sprite sheet, strip or grid as an animation,
  one frame per cell (columns x rows)
- join <image> <image> … [--as sheet|rows|animation] [--columns n] — pictures
  or animations as one sprite sheet, one per row, or one animation
- scale <image> --by 4 — the same picture or animation bigger, each pixel a
  4x4 block (a sticker, a print); nothing is redrawn
A result comes back as an image in the reply AND as a no-auth URL the reply
prints, `/mcp/pixel-tools/<id>/image.png` (`frames.png` for the frames of a
multi-frame one) — so a sheet you joined is both readable inline and
downloadable. Sheets hold at most 1024 px a side; `join` refuses a larger
one rather than shrinking the art, and says how many frames do fit.
Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`.
Authoring: `edit <id> --changes '[…]'` applies exact pixel operations and
`draw <id> --recipe '{…}'` builds or revises a layered scene; both take JSON
whose fields are NOT listed here. Colours in that JSON are always `#RRGGBB`
or `#RRGGBBAA` with alpha `00` or `ff` — `rgb()` and bare hex are refused,
and nothing strips the `#`, since argv is a JSON list rather than a shell
line. Every `edit` change carries `operation`, `layer`, `frames` (ONE-based)
and `reason`; coordinates are zero-based and a `region` is `[x0,y0,x1,y1]`
inclusive. Then its own fields: `patch_pixels` takes `pixels`, a list of
`[x,y,expected,replacement]` (1-10000, each assigned only where the pixel
already holds `expected`, so a mismatch fails the pass); `copy_region` takes
`source_layer`, `source_frame`, `region`, `at` `[x,y]`; `map_colors` takes
`region` and `colors` `{"#from":"#to"}` (alpha must match); `flood_fill`
`seed`/`expected`/`color`; `brush` `points` plus `color`; `outline` `mode`
(outside|inside|recolor|erase). The full contracts and any command's flags
are one free call away: `describe edits | paint | outline | draw | animation
| motion | scenes | review`, `<command> -h`, `describe cli`.
Free for subscribers.

PixelLab AI-powered pixel art generation service.

Use of this service is subject to PixelLab's Terms of Service:
https://pixellab.ai/termsofservice

This MCP server provides programmatic access to generate:
- Characters with multiple directional views
- Character animations
- Isometric tiles
- Top-down tilesets for game maps
- Sidescroller tilesets for platformer games

All generation operations are non-blocking and return job IDs for status tracking.
Requires PixelLab subscription (with credit fallback support).

**Pixel tools (free, exact, you are the artist)**: one command line, pixelart_workbench(argv=[...]), inspects, edits, draws and animates pixel art by your own decisions; combine it with the AI tools above. Start with pixelart_workbench(argv=['describe', 'start'], mode='low'|'high') — low acts directly with few tokens, high plans out loud and reviews every frame. Animated effects (spells, hits, explosions, auras): vfx_workbench(argv=['describe', 'start']) — same ids, exports to the user's My effects.

**Git access**: Clone and push game project source code with standard git.
Use `list_projects` to see your projects and their git clone URLs.

exec tool declaration:
```ts
declare const tools: { mcp__pixellab__pixelart_workbench(args: {
  // One command line, e.g. 'lint <drawing_id> --rules outline_gap' or ['edit', '<id>', '--changes', '[…]']. Omit it for the playbook. A subject is an id or an image reference — never a file path; the server writes the output and returns a new id. A reference is `character:<id>:<direction>` for a rotation, `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` for every frame of that animation (the display name, type or [group: ...] id get_character prints), the same two forms for `object:<id>` (a one-direction object's direction is the literal `unknown`), `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>`, `upload:<id>`, a data URL, an https link or base64. That is how a stored animation's pixels come back inline without downloading anything. Start with 'describe cli' for the full command list.
  argv?: string | Array<string> | null;
  // low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.
  mode?: "low" | "high";
  // What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.
  notes?: string | null;
}): Promise<CallToolResult>; };
```

content.text:
# Revising a drawing — `changes` and `inspect`

After `draw` renders, revise with small, reasoned changes instead of
rewriting the recipe. Each call appends to the drawing's change list, rebuilds
everything from the original sources, and shows a before/after with change
masks against the drawing you revised.

```
pixelart_workbench(argv=["draw", "--drawing", "<id>", "--changes", "[ …operations… ]"])
pixelart_workbench(argv=["draw", "--drawing", "<id>", "--inspect", "[ …crops… ]"])
```

Every operation needs `operation`, `frames` (one-based) and `reason`.

**Pose / drawing** — `set_node` overrides a node on chosen frames (`at`, `pivot`,
`angle`, `opacity`, `visible`, or a replacement `draw` list):

```json
{"operation": "set_node", "view": "south", "node": "arm", "frames": [3],
 "values": {"angle": -140, "at": {"node": "root", "point": [1, 0]}},
 "reason": "The raised arm clips the head; move it out and lower it a little."}
```

**Structure** — these two edit the drawing itself rather than chosen frames,
so they take `view` and `reason`, not `frames` (only `add_node` has an optional
`frames`: the frames it shows on):
- `add_node` — `{"operation": "add_node", "view": "south", "node": "spark",
  "values": {"layer": "fx", "at": [30, 12], "draw": [ … ]}, "frames": [3, 4],
  "reason": "…"}`. With `frames` it shows on those frames only; `after` names the
  node it draws after. No placeholder nodes needed.
- `set_track` — `{"operation": "set_track", "view": "south", "node": "arm",
  "property": "angle", "keys": [[1, 0], [3, -140]], "reason": "…"}` replaces
  that node's track for that property (optional `interpolation`/`anchor`, as in
  the recipe). Works on a view timed by `tracks`, or on a still view, which it
  gives its first track; a view timed by `poses`/`frames` changes with `set_node`.
  Tracks run first; a `set_node` on the same frames overrides them.

To remove a node, send the recipe again without it — a fresh `draw` costs the
same as a revision.

**Timing** — `{"operation": "duration", "frames": [3], "milliseconds": 200,
"reason": "Hold the peak longer."}` (10 ms steps; applies to every view).

**Pixels on a layer** — every `edit` operation works here too, with
`view` and a layer **name** as printed in the response (`"Body - right arm"`):

```json
{"operation": "patch_pixels", "view": "south", "layer": "Body - right arm",
 "frames": [2, 3], "pixels": [[43, 22, "#f0c8a0ff", "#221c1aff"]],
 "reason": "Close the outline gap at the elbow."}
```

Guards check the colour ON THAT LAYER, which can differ from the flattened
image — read it first with a layer inspection. Raster fixes run after posing, so
a later `set_node` can move pixels out from under an old patch: re-inspect.
Mirrored views follow their original automatically; edit the original.

**Inspect** — enlarged crops of the current render:

```json
[{"view": "south", "mode": "body", "frames": [2, 3, 4], "region": [30, 10, 50, 40], "scale": 10},
 {"view": "south", "mode": "layer", "layer": "Body - right arm", "frames": [3], "region": [36, 12, 48, 30]}]
```

`full` = everything, `body` = body layers only, `layer` = one layer, and also
returns that layer's exact colours per pixel (palette-indexed) for guards.

The engine contract below was written for its command line: its decision
envelope (`candidate_id` / `decision: "edit"|"inspect"|"finish"`) is what these
two parameters replace — send only the operations. `finish` is not needed; the
user judges the result. Ignore file paths, commands and experiment links.


---

The engine contract below was written for its command line. Here: `edit <id> --changes` is its PNG/GIF worker — send only the `changes` list (no `version` / `source_sha256` envelope; `layer` defaults to "image"). `draw` is its animation job — a `recipe` is a job + scene, `--changes` and `--inspect` replace its edit/inspect decisions, and finish is not needed. Ignore file paths, commands and experiment links; the server fills every path field.

---

# Python animation jobs

Render and revise layered pixel animation with Python, NumPy and Pillow. No Aseprite, display, GPU, model service or API key is required. The worker renders JSON-controlled animation; a separate caller supplies visual judgments.

For new actions, use `python-drawing` with a `layered-drawing-v1` scene. It supports arbitrary frame counts, named source parts, drawing primitives, reusable poses, anchored equipment and JSON node edits. Read the [drawing scene format](DRAWING_SCENES.md) and use the [eight-frame archer test](../experiments/python-drawing-v2/README.md) as a compact example. New artwork and motion still need to be designed and reviewed; the worker does not turn a text prompt into animation by itself.

The older `python-articulated` backend and `articulated-burst-v1` template remain a regression fixture for Umbra Core. That template has a fixed 44-frame phase schedule and should not be selected automatically for unrelated actions.

For walk cycles and other repeated motion, the [cyclic motion workflow](MOTION_WORKFLOW.md) adds source-part selection, compact pose tracks, onion-skin evidence and foot-anchor checks. It compiles into the same drawing backend. Identical full/body review sheets are deduplicated and declared in `equivalent_evidence_modes`; both underlying exports remain available.

## Run a job

From the workspace root, with `server/requirements.txt` installed:

```sh
python tools/animation_job.py build experiments/python-drawing-v2/final-job.json --out experiments/my-animation/run-001
python tools/animation_job.py decide experiments/my-animation/run-001 decision.json --out experiments/my-animation/run-002
```

The first command renders; the second accepts `inspect` or `edit` decisions. `finish` records a review in the existing run and does not take `--out`. Output directories must be new and inside the workspace. Existing runs and input pixels remain intact. Job asset paths resolve from the workspace root; part-map paths resolve from the scene directory. Supply trusted job configuration and asset paths from your application, not arbitrary public request bodies.

For a queue worker, import `prepare_job`, `build`, and `decide` from `tools.animation_job`. `build(prepare_job(job_path), output_path)` returns the result dictionary. `decide(run_path, decision_dict, output_path)` applies validated structured feedback. The CLI and Python functions share the same implementation. A web endpoint, queue and storage adapter are outside this prototype.

The [small sample](../experiments/python-drawing-v2/README.md) documents the drawing comparison; the [older reproduction](../experiments/streamlined-animation-v1/README.md) remains available. For a Linux worker image, build from the repository root with `docker build -f server/animation.Dockerfile -t pixel-animation .`. Mount prepared input jobs under `/app/jobs`, then run `pixel-animation build /app/jobs/job.json --out /app/jobs/run-001`. The Docker definition has not been built or deployed here.

## What stays reusable

| Component | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `server/pixel_renderer.py` | Pixel rasterization, layers, polygon transforms, two-bone IK and common shapes |
| `server/pixel_ops.py` | Normal RGBA compositing and inverse-sampled bitmap transforms |
| `server/pixel_edits.py` | Guarded pixel patches, simultaneous color tables, reference-region copying and exact palette inspection |
| `server/drawing_renderer.py` | General JSON drawing, source cutouts, named poses and anchors |
| `server/articulated_renderer.py` | Current action template, source-part posing, VFX and direction mirroring |
| Scene JSON and label PNGs | Character-specific pivots, limbs, source-part assignment, pose keys, colors and layer order |
| `tools/animation_job.py` | Validation, rendering, exports, provenance, comparisons and review decisions |
| Model or human reviewer | Motion intent, preservation judgments, observations and bounded edits |

Layer archives are numeric `.npz` files with arrays shaped `[frame, y, x, RGBA]`, loaded with `numpy.load(path, allow_pickle=False)`. `frames.json` maps archive keys to named body/VFX layers and includes durations, tags and drawing-node anchors. Exports include full and body-only PNG sheets, GIFs and a shared HTML viewer with one clock, integer zoom and consistent backgrounds.

The drawing backend supports normal alpha compositing and node opacity. PNG sheets and layer archives retain partial alpha. GIF cannot: declare an opaque `gif_background` such as `#52596e` to produce an explicitly matted GIF preview when needed. Otherwise partial-alpha GIF export is rejected. A GIF exceeding the exact encoder's palette capacity is skipped (reported as `gif_omitted`) instead of being silently quantized; the PNG sheets and layers stay exact. The legacy burst backend still uses binary alpha.

For requested outline styling, use the [outline operations](OUTLINE_TOOLS.md). Jobs default to `source_bookends_exact: true`. Set it to `false` in a trusted job only when the requested restyle intentionally changes the first/rest pose; raw first/last equality remains in `reference_comparisons` in the result and review packet. This does not disable protected-region, palette, timing or export checks. The existing `body_palette_exact` setting controls whether new body colors are permitted.

## Visual feedback loop

1. Inspect the original artwork, the intended action and all supplied directions. Preserve identity, native pixels and source palette. Record protected features and intended effects before editing.
2. Build a candidate. Open `packet.json` and **attach its PNG evidence** to the model, or open the files directly in Codex. Generating a packet does not send images or constitute review.
3. Review numbered full/body sheets covering every frame, 10x nearest-neighbor source views, and palette swatches. The packet includes source, effect and actual output palettes. Sheets default to 2x to fit useful frame groups. Request 8–10x matching crops for ambiguous details instead of enlarging an entire animation indiscriminately.
4. Return `inspect`, `edit` or `finish`. Batch related edits. An edit rebuilds from pinned inputs into a new run, propagates original-view edits to mirrors, and creates changed-pixel counts, numbered masks, before/after key-frame PNGs and comparison GIFs against its immediate parent.
5. Inspect the new evidence and affected neighbors. Check body motion separately from effects. Check playback, light/dark backgrounds and the loop seam in `index.html`. A model receiving a GIF file must not assume it has watched every frame.
6. Once the motion works, review pixel polish separately. Inspect joints, overlapping parts, cloth/equipment boundaries, outlines and small detached clusters in matching 8–10x crops with adjacent poses. Moved source cutouts can carry neighboring material pixels even when palette and renderer-parity checks pass. Use exact layer inspection and batch guarded `patch_pixels` for observed local defects; save the patches after posing so rebuilds retain them. Open the new comparison and change masks, then check all final frames and the loop again. Do not force edits when no defect is observed or send one model call per pixel.
7. Accept only after technical checks and visual review pass. If playback or another required check is unavailable, record a `partial` result with the remaining issue. Stop after two edit/review passes without observed improvement and return the best reviewed candidate with limitations; this is a caller policy, not an automatic worker loop.

The worker does not invoke a model. This keeps subscription testing and a future API reviewer interchangeable. It also means CPU renders use zero model tokens; development and visual review still consume tokens. Pixel equality to a reference proves reproduction, not that an unfamiliar animation meets the user's intent.

Use the [compact review prompt](animation-review.prompt.md) with the user's intent, the operation contract and the current packet. Subsequent turns need the latest decision and new evidence rather than the renderer source or the full development conversation.

## Decision contract

All decisions contain the exact `candidate_id` from `result.json`. Frames are **one-based**. Pixel coordinates are **zero-based**, relative to the padded canvas; rectangles include both endpoints. Unknown fields, operations, layer names and invalid bounds are rejected. Colors are `#RRGGBB` or `#RRGGBBAA`, with alpha `00` or `ff`.

Legacy `pixels` and `replace_color` edits retain the binary-alpha restriction. Drawing-node commands can contain partial alpha. The [pixel editing contract](PIXEL_EDIT_TOOLS.md) adds `patch_pixels`, `map_colors`, `copy_region`, and exact layer/palette inspection to `python-drawing`, plus a direct PNG/GIF entry point. These share one implementation and report per-operation pixel changes. For pose and drawing changes, use `set_node`:

```json
{"operation":"set_node","view":"south","node":"bow","frames":[2,7],"values":{"at":[55,48]},"reason":"Move the rising bow clear of the hair; its anchored hand follows."}
```

Node edits can change `at`, `pivot`, `angle`, `opacity`, `visible`, or `draw`. A replacement `draw` list can redraw a shape, restore a source region, or change outlines without writing Python. Anchor cycles and unsupported commands are rejected. The scene format describes the actual supported commands. `pose_key` below applies only to the older articulated backend.

Inspection:

```json
{
  "candidate_id": "COPY_FROM_RESULT",
  "decision": "inspect",
  "inspections": [{
    "view": "east", "mode": "body", "frames": [21, 22, 23],
    "region": [120, 70, 159, 109], "scale": 10,
    "reason": "Check the hand and torso through release."
  }]
}
```

An edit has `candidate_id`, `decision: "edit"` and a nonempty `changes` array. Supported change objects:

```json
[
  {"operation":"duration","frames":[22],"milliseconds":80,"reason":"Release needs a longer hold."},
  {"operation":"pose_key","frames":[22],"values":{"torso_lean_deg":-10,"arm_spread":0.9},"reason":"The release pose is too extended."},
  {"operation":"pixels","view":"east","layer":"VFX - sparks","frames":[23],"pixels":[[180,90,"#00000000"]],"reason":"Remove an observed stray spark."},
  {"operation":"replace_color","view":"east","layer":"VFX - core light","frames":[22],"region":[120,70,159,109],"from":"#ffffff","to":"#ffe5b5","reason":"Use the intended warm highlight."}
]
```

These are syntax examples, not instructions to apply those edits to the sample. `pixels` and `replace_color` address original views only; mirrors follow automatically. `duration` applies to every direction, in 10 ms steps. `pose_key` edits an existing shared keyframe using any of `forward_root`, `crouch`, `torso_lean_deg`, `arm_fold`, `arm_spread`, `foot_stride`, `foot_lift`, `head_counter_rotation_deg`. Root-motion metadata follows the edited curve. This template's native rest frames and fixed effect phases still apply.

A finish decision contains exactly:

- `candidate_id`, `decision: "finish"`, `status: "accepted"` or `"partial"`.
- `reviewed_evidence`: map of actually viewed relative PNG paths to their supplied SHA-256 hashes.
- `visual_checks`: boolean judgments for `source_fidelity`, `articulation`, `equipment_contact`, `effects`, `clipping`, `loop_transition`.
- `playback_verified`: boolean, and `unresolved`: list of remaining issues.

Acceptance requires all listed evidence, all visual checks true, verified playback, passing technical checks and no unresolved issues. File hashes reject stale decisions and changed deliverables. The review is explicitly **caller-attested**: JSON cannot prove that a human or model actually examined the images.

## Validation

Run `python -m unittest server.test_drawing_renderer tools.test_animation_job tools.test_drawing_pipeline -v`. Protected regions in a view can enforce exact pixels or preserve the original visible source pixels throughout the body timeline. Use them for features intended to stay still; palette equality alone does not detect erased details.

`tools/check_animation_viewer.py PAGE --out NEW_DIR --compare 0 2` performs optional local browser verification, including playback, loop crossing, integer zoom and rendered pixel comparison. It uses development-only Playwright and Edge; neither is a worker dependency. Aseprite reference generation is also test-only, via `tools/prepare_drawing_reference.py` and `tools/aseprite/reference_drawing.lua`. Their comparison uses the same resolved geometry and source cutouts, so it does not establish independent animation-design quality or complete Aseprite feature parity.
